analysis.one_liner: Lets paid-off medical debt and on-time medical payment plans count as positive items on credit reports.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on October 1, 2024, with one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and never received a committee vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that companies holding medical debt could report paid-off or settled medical bills, and consumers keeping up with medical payment plans, as positive items on credit reports and credit scores. Credit bureaus and score providers would have to build procedures to include that information. The bill died in committee without ever being voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who have paid off or settled medical debt, or who are paying medical bills on a payment plan, would get credit history credit for it instead of having that debt simply disappear or linger as a collection. Roughly, that means the large share of Americans who carry medical debt and whose borrowing costs for a car, apartment, or mortgage depend on their credit file.

how_it_helps.text: Medical debt owners would be allowed to furnish information showing a consumer paid or settled a medical debt at least a year before the credit report, turning a past negative item into a positive one.
A furnisher and consumer could enter a medical debt payment plan, and the consumer's satisfactory performance on that plan could be reported as positive credit information.

Credit bureaus and credit score providers would be required to adopt reasonable procedures so this positive medical-debt information is included in consumer reports, used in credit scores, and provided to lenders fairly.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and credit score providers would bear the cost of building systems to accept and use this positive medical-debt data. The obligations on them are procedures, not heavy mandates, since the bill says furnishers 'may' report this information, not that they must.

drawbacks.text: The bill is permissive: it says a furnisher 'may' furnish positive medical-debt information, not that it must, so there is no guarantee consumers would actually see the benefit.

The bill would reopen the door to medical debt appearing on credit reports even after it is paid or settled, if paid off more than a year before the report, at a time when the credit bureaus' own policy and regulators were moving the other way by removing paid medical collections entirely; even labeled 'positive,' the presence of a medical collection account can still raise questions from lenders.

Whether a consumer on a payment plan is 'meeting the obligations' is decided by the furnisher itself, giving the debt owner discretion that could produce disputes or be used as leverage to encourage payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea is sound for consumers in the abstract: paying medical bills on time is exactly the kind of behavior credit scores are supposed to reward, and today it counts for nothing. But the bill is a light-touch version of that idea. Because reporting is optional, a debt collector could sign a consumer to a plan, then simply choose not to furnish the positive data, while the bill simultaneously lets long-paid medical debt reappear on reports. A stronger version would make positive reporting mandatory and bar paid medical debt from reports altogether.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, sat there with no hearings, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) introduced the bill on October 1, 2024, joined by Rep. Perez (D), and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill's only recorded action was that referral; the action history shows no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote afterward.
The bill was introduced in the final three months of a two-year Congress, when most bills referred to committee are never taken up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers with medical debt gained nothing because the bill never advanced, but credit bureaus and medical debt collectors were also spared the new reporting procedures and the reopening of paid-debt reporting; the practical winner is the status quo, in which on-time medical payments count for nothing on credit scores.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; the bill simply expired

for.name: Rep. Don Bacon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 1, 2024, to allow positive reporting of paid and on-schedule medical debt.

for.name: Rep. Perez
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one sponsor from each party.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to, chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no committee action after the referral, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and no recorded opposition, but with only two supporters it never progressed far enough for any partisan fight to occur.

industries.industry: Medical debt collectors and debt buyers
industries.note: They would gain a new legal authority to report paid and on-schedule medical debt as positive credit information, which could help their customers rebuild credit but also keeps medical debts on credit files longer and lets the collector, not the consumer, decide when plan performance qualifies.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and credit score providers
industries.note: They would have to build procedures to accept and score positive medical-debt data, a modest cost, while their scores remain the gatekeeper through which any benefit flows.
Providers holding their own patient debt could furnish positive payment-plan data, which may give patients a modest incentive to keep up with medical payment plans.
